claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are homogeneous, equiatomic solid solutions.
Premelting and melting in these nanoparticles are governed by incipient chemical segregation.
Cu atoms preferentially migrate to surface and near-surface regions at elevated temperatures.
Surface Cu enrichment creates localized regions of reduced cohesive energy.
Regions with reduced cohesive energy melt earlier than the nanoparticle bulk.
Differences in elemental interfacial energies drive atomic redistribution at elevated temperatures.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other principal constituents of the alloy.
Cu's lower melting point promotes its segregation to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu segregation lowers the local melting temperature and initiates premelting.
Slower heating provides more time for atomic redistribution.
Particles heated at 1 K/min will show earlier and more pronounced premelting than particles heated at moderate or faster rates such as 10 K/min.
Premelting will be observable as liquid-like surface layers and endothermic DSC events.
Rapid cooling will freeze in compositional inhomogeneities generated during heating.
The frozen-in inhomogeneity will be observable as nanoscale Cu enrichment at the surface.
Moderate-rate baseline particles will display a delayed and less pronounced premelting onset relative to slowly heated particles.
The proposed comparison uses heating rates of approximately 1 K/min and 10 K/min and contrasts rapid with slow cooling under an inert atmosphere.
The hypothesis is limited to initially homogeneous, equiatomic particles whose sizes permit appreciable surface diffusion and atomic rearrangement in an inert atmosphere.
Extreme particle-size variation or environmental changes may introduce additional effects not represented by the hypothesis.
Failure to observe both the predicted heating-rate dependence and measurable Cu surface enrichment would falsify the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism.
